title: Merrit and the Whispering Willow
markdown:
The Azure Spine: villages clinging to cliffs like barnacles, paths of rope and dark whispering pine. There lived Merrit, a wizard whose heart was as vast as the sky and whose laboratory often looked as if a whirlwind had dropped in for tea: bubbling potions, teetering scrolls, good intentions in every spill.

With him, always, Pip: a ferret of astonishing cleverness and even more astonishing quickness, fur like polished acorns, eyes like tiny knowing stars. Pip understood Merrit better than Merrit understood himself, a truth usually admitted after tripping over a scroll.

A peculiar problem: Hoot, the wise old owl of quiet thought and excellent judgment, had flown out for the world’s tastiest grubs and had not returned. So Merrit, Pip chattering encouragement from his shoulder, descended to the bustling Mountain Market in search of a new friend—someone, Pip squeaked, for afternoon tea and dust bunnies.

The market was colour, smell, and a roar that could make a dragon sneeze. Glowing fungi, tinkling chimes, whirring contraptions. Merrit, who preferred quiet reading, felt a nervous tickle. His magic was strong. His disarray was charming and public.

In the middle of the crowd, Grungle: a goblin, skin like damp moss, grin wide as a crack in a boulder, stall piled with things that looked important and possibly dangerous.

“Ah, wizard!” Voice like rattling pebbles. “A companion? A familiar of the finest sort? Grungle has just the thing.”

Merrit tried to remember what made a good familiar: sharp eyes, quiet flight, good advice. He looked at the offerings.

“A magnificent eagle?” Grungle boomed, holding up a ruffled chicken with a stern unblinking stare. “Regal gaze! Mighty talons!”

Merrit blinked. “That is a very cross hen. Very cross indeed.”

“A misunderstanding!” Twinkling mischief. He swapped the hen for a small fluffy creature that puffed up indignantly. “A majestic miniature bear! Fierce and loyal!”

“That,” Pip whispered, nose almost touching it, “looks like a very angry dandelion puff. One that’s had a very bad morning.”

“And a potent one at that!” Grungle, unbothered. Merrit’s brow furrowed. He loved discovering new things. This market was testing his orderly mind, which had never been very orderly.

The parade continued: a singing mushroom that wailed, a stone that buzzed oddly, a grumpy gnome who only complained about the weather. Merrit felt out of his depth. A sigh stirred dust in a sunbeam.

Pip was not flustered. He watched Grungle, still. Whiskers twitched; he nudged Merrit’s ear. “He never offers what you want. He offers what he thinks you need, and it’s always just… off.”

Merrit paused. He looked past the stall to a quiet woman selling fragrant herbs, a lantern’s long shadows, pine and damp earth holding its breath.

He needed a familiar, yes—but perhaps not one that flew or scampered. Perhaps not a creature at all.

Grungle held up a long slender branch. Silver leaves rustled with no breeze. “A Whispering Willow branch! Excellent for very quiet contemplation. It holds secrets you can whisper to it!”

Merrit’s heart leapt. Wizards said such a branch listened, absorbed thoughts, offered gentle guidance. Not a creature. Quiet deep magic. And Pip—he realised with a surge of ordinary love—was already the companion. The branch would be for spells, a silent friend for studies.

“That is not a prophecy, Grungle. That is a very ambitious shopping list, and I am here to fulfil it.”

Confusion, then grudging respect. Goblins knew cleverness. He accepted Merrit’s pouch of shimmering moon-gems with a nod.

Merrit walked home, Pip trotting, tail high, the branch held carefully. On the desk it seemed to hum, silver leaves like a soft whisper. Hoot would come back when the grubs ran out. Until then the tower had a ferret, a willow, and slightly fewer wrong purchases than Grungle had hoped.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing fantasy story for middle-grade readers
